newsitem.title: USA: Nobel laureate Edward Purcell dead at 84.
newsitem.headline: Nobel laureate Edward Purcell dead at 84.

text.p: Edward Purcell, who shared the 1952 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on nuclear magnetic resonance, now commonly used in medical diagnosis, died at his Cambridge home, Harvard University said on Sunday. He was 84.

An experimental physicist, Purcell and his co-workers, notably Robert Pound and Nicholaas (cq) Bloembergen, winner of the 1981 Nobel Prize in Physics, developed the basic theory of nuclear magnetic relaxation.

The concept of negative absolute temperature introduced by their experiments found later application in the development of masers -- a device operating at microwave frequency for amplifying electro-magnetic waves by stimulated emission of radiation.
In 1951 Purcell and his colleagues detected radio waves from hydrogen atoms in interstellar space. Radio astronomers have since used the discovery to map galaxies.

He shared the 1952 Nobel Prize with Stanford University's Felix Block for their independent discovery of nuclear magnetic resonance, widely used today in medical diagnosis -- magnetic resonance imaging -- to study molecular structures and to measure magnetic fields.
During the Second World War, Purcell headed a group at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Radiation Laboratory which developed advanced microwave radar.
He served on several national advisory committees under Presidents Eisenhower, Kennedy and Johnson.
Purcell, who died on Friday, is survived by his wife, Beth, and two sons, Dennis and Frank, his brother, Robert, and four grandchildren.
